**Verdict:** No. Paul Graham would tell you not to start a startup in college. He'd tell you to keep working on the side project as a project, and to make it a company only if it takes off by itself. At that point you'd have to choose between dropping out and abandoning it.

His reasoning: a startup takes over your whole life, so you can't really be a student and a founder at the same time. Twenty isn't the best age to found a company, and waiting costs you nothing. He's also very clear that side projects like yours are where the best startups come from.

**Based on:** he said it. He gave this advice directly to Stanford students in 2014. His August 2026 essay keeps the rule but puts more weight on the exception. That essay is written to universities, not to students.

**Why he'd say it**
- He's blunt about it: "Do not start a startup in college." and "though starting a startup could be a good thing to do at some point, 20 is not the optimal time to do it." ([Before the Startup, 2014 @ 18:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s))
- **Being a student and running a startup don't mix:** "you can't start up a startup as a student, because if you start a startup you're not a student anymore." In 2026 he still says "Running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student." ([2014 @ 18:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1102s); [How Universities Should Prepare Founders, 2026](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))
- **Waiting costs you nothing:** "You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." He thinks your early twenties are for exploration that success would take away, and his example is Zuckerberg: "Facebook is running him as much as he is running Facebook." ([2014 @ 21:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s), [@ 20:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1240s))
- **Your excitement isn't the test. Whether it takes off without being pushed is.** He gives the exception and then narrows it right away: if you have "some side project that takes off like Facebook did. Then you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it. But usually the way startups take off is for the founders to make them take off. It's gratuitously stupid to do that at 20." ([2014 @ 21:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s))
- **He still thinks you should build the project.** In 2026 he says "Projects are the best source of knowledge, the best source of founding teams, and the best source of startup ideas," and he notes that Microsoft and Meta "both got started during reading period at Harvard." In 2014 he said following real interests energetically is "the best way to prepare yourself for a start-up." ([2026](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html); [2014 @ 27:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1677s))
- **If you're unsure whether you could do it:** "the only way to find out is to try, just not now." ([2014 @ 23:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1438s))

**What he's done:** He co-founded YC partly as a summer alternative for students. His 2026 essay asks universities to give students more free time precisely so that side projects like yours can turn into startups.

**What would change his answer:** the project takes off by itself, with users growing it without you pushing. Then he says "maybe it's reasonable to run with it," and in 2026 he spells out that the choice is "either that or drop out." The vault never shows him naming a threshold for "takes off." My guess, based on his habit of asking founders about growth rate first, is that he'd look at whether usage is growing on its own, not at how excited you are.

**Tension worth knowing:** in 2023 he said the young are the ones who "can afford to risk trying it to find out" and that you should "start taking risks early" ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). In the 2014 talk he weighs that against college and still says "just not now." He's YC's founder, so his advice about when and how students should start is not neutral.

**Verdict:** Yes, you should go, but you don't have to stay. Paul Graham said this in a talk he gave in Stockholm (29 April 2026), to an audience asking your exact question. His advice is to go to Silicon Valley for a while, ideally through YC, and then come back.

**Based on:** said it (directly, to a Stockholm audience)

Source: *Paul Graham, Founder of Y Combinator, Live from Stockholm*, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8

**What he said**
- **His answer:** "Should I go there? And the answer is the same now as it always is. Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go." ([@ 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s)) He says every field has one center, like Paris for painting or Hollywood for movies. Today the center for startups is Silicon Valley.
- **Why go:** you'll be among more and better people. "You get the best peers… The people are better, and there's also a lot more of them." ([@ 1:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=69s)) You'll also have more chance meetings that turn out to be valuable, and things move faster.
- **The biggest reason is what it does to you:** "the biggest advantage of moving to one of these centers is not what it does for you, but what it does to you." ([@ 8:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=499s)) Up close, the people who built huge companies stop looking out of reach. The goal goes from impossible to merely hard.
- **Investors:** "Investors outside Silicon Valley implicitly assume that any local startup is second rate. It's not a uniquely Swedish problem." If you go to the Valley, that works in reverse: "You automatically rise in investors' opinion." ([@ 6:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=399s))
- **Coming back is part of the plan:** "you should go for a bit and then come back... as long as you do actually come back, that's one of the best things you can do to help Sweden to help Stockholm thrive as a startup hub." ([@ 16:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=970s)) He thinks the best way to do this is "Surely the optimal way to go to Silicon Valley for a bit and then come back is to do YC." ([@ 17:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1036s))

**The cost of going home**
- He says YC's data shows that "startups that go back home after YC are only about half as likely to become unicorns." He then discounts that number for three reasons ([@ 18:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1137s)):
  - Selection bias: the founders who stay tend to be more confident and determined to begin with.
  - It measures valuation, not how well the company actually does, and Bay Area companies raise at higher valuations.
  - "even if you only do half as well, that's still pretty good." ([@ 19:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1170s))
- Life matters too: "Where do you want your kids to grow up? Eventually, that becomes the most important question." ([@ 20:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1204s))

**What would change his answer:** whether Stockholm reaches a critical mass of founders. He thinks the job of "Silicon Valley of Europe" is "still up for grabs." He also said: "All you need is a place founders want to live and a critical mass of them. Stockholm, I can tell from being here, is the kind of place founders want to live." ([@ 21:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1269s)) If Stockholm reaches that point, his reason for leaving gets weaker. The way he expects it to get there is founders going and coming back.

**Caveats:**
- He's YC's founder recommending YC, and he says so himself: "I know it will sound like I'm talking my own book at this point." ([@ 17:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1036s))
- The "half as likely" figure is YC's internal data, and the talk shows no method behind it.
- Sam Altman, another YC figure in the vault, takes a softer line in a July 2026 talk. He agrees moving was clearly right in the past, but says he has "less of an intuition" about it now.

**Verdict:** Seibel would tell you to stop fundraising and go back to building. He'd see months of pitching, deck polishing and follow-up meetings as a "low leverage fundraise". He calls that a waste of time, and he made the same mistake himself at Justin.tv. His view is that if you build a company investors chase, the round almost takes care of itself.

**Based on:** something he said directly. His October 2026 episode with Dalton Caldwell is about exactly this situation.

**Why he'd say it**

- **Months of pitching is a drag, not progress.** "if you just think about how much time is wasted, it's like a it's like a drag on the industry." ([7TU636F_yVQ @ 6:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s))
- **Polishing the deck is the wrong thing to work on.** "if you can invest that time in making your company something that investors will chase after versus decksmithing, you're you're playing into the odds versus playing out of the odds." ([@ 10:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=603s)) He said the same in 2019: "spending all that time on a pitch deck is not as valuable as spending your time building anything that you can give to a customer." ([1hHMwLxN6EM @ 11:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=671s))
- **The odds favor companies investors chase.** He asked investors what share of their deals they chase versus what comes "in the front door". The answers ranged from 80/20 to 90/10 chased. A polished cold pitch is competing for the smallest slice.
- **The follow-up meetings may not mean what you hope.** The episode describes investors who string founders along as if they were buying an option: they keep meeting in case you take off, and the meetings themselves make that less likely ([@ 8:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=537s)). The vault can't tell whether Seibel or Caldwell said that part, but Seibel's reply is "I'm so not aligned with that."
- **The real question is leverage, not pitch quality.** At YC office hours, when founders asked what should go in the deck, the hosts answered by asking how much leverage they had. In practice that means: are you growing, and could you walk away from any one investor?
- **A "no" from investors doesn't mean the idea is bad** (applying his principle). He says Coinbase wouldn't exist if its founder had taken "the demo day signal the investor signal of oh we don't want to give you money and quit" ([Jcuqq48CNj8 @ 12:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=723s)). The vault attributes that line to him with medium confidence. So months of rejections are a reason to change where your time goes, not a reason to quit.

**What he's done**

- **Justin.tv:** he spent about eight months trying to raise. With two months of runway left and clearly no money coming, the team switched to making the company profitable: "we got to figure out how to make this thing profitable or we're going to die." He says they got more done in those two months than in all the months of "slinging decks".
- **Socialcam:** when it was the #2 app in the App Store, one of its pitch decks was basically "here's some questions you can ask us," plus graphs going up and to the right ([@ 9:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=570s)). The deck barely mattered.

**What would change his answer:** real traction. If you're growing fast and have clear proof points, he'd say go ahead and raise, quickly and without much prep. The episode argues that a short, almost improvised raise at the very end beats months of preparation. If you aren't launched or growing, extra deck work is what the episode calls possibly "the biggest waste of your time."

**Caveat:** the 2026 episode is sponsored by Standard Capital, the Series A fund Caldwell co-founded. Its pitch to founders is a capped time commitment for applicants, so this advice also helps its sponsor. Still, it's the same advice PG gave in 2014 ("the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well … and then simply tell investors so"), and Seibel's Justin.tv story is his own experience.

**Verdict:** Seibel would tell you both to stop paying lawyers to write letters and settle this yourselves within a week. Your cofounder gives back most of his vested stock and ends up with roughly 1–2% (possibly less) because he's leaving inside the first year. You give him reasonable severance, you both sign clean no-fault paperwork, and you part ways. His reasoning is that before product-market fit the stock is worth close to nothing, so a legal fight over it is a fight about ego that leaves you with legal bills and a reputation.

**Based on:** said it. He describes almost exactly your situation in the July 2026 Dalton + Michael episode on cofounder breakups ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U)).

**Why he'd say it**
- **Your stock is worth nothing yet, so the lawyers are the only ones gaining.** "in a situation where you're having a co-founder breakup and the stock is worth nothing, paying lawyers a bunch of money makes no sense." ([@ 11:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=696s)) He adds that "a lawyer can suck up infinite amount of your ... anger and monetize it." ([@ 12:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=727s)) He says he's seen a departing founder end up in debt over a company worth nothing.
- **Having vested doesn't change his answer.** "If you are pre-product market fit, even if any of the founders leaving, even if you vested a lot of stock, you should probably willing to give a lot back." ([@ 20:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1250s)) He also gives numbers: "After a number of years, 5% typical. Under a year, 1%, 2%, sometimes less than 1%." ([@ 21:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1282s))
- **The whole thing should take a week and about $2,000.** "Do reasonable severance, sign clean paperwork and and peace out ... you could do that whole thing in a week and spend like $2,000." ([@ 18:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1119s))
- **The pitch to your cofounder:** he walks away with a free option on the company, while you carry all the risk. "Like, you get to hedge. The founder staying doesn't." ([@ 15:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=921s)) The leaver should "understand that you want to motivate the team that remains to make that stock worth something." ([@ 21:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1282s)) If he keeps a big stake in a company nobody is motivated to build, his stake is worth nothing too.
- **The pitch to you, if you're the one staying:** be generous, and don't cast yourself as the victim. He warns that lawyers who tell the staying founder to protect themselves are how that founder "inadvertently ... triggers the fight." ([@ 18:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1086s)) Your team is also watching how you handle this: "how you treat this person is how the people around you think they're going to get treated." ([@ 21:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1282s)) And "it is so cheap to be nice." ([@ 17:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1053s))
- **Stop arguing about who was right.** "If you made a list of all the things we screwed up in our company, it would be way longer than the things you're pissed at your co-founder about." ([@ 21:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1314s)) If you bring in a mediator, "don't make them the judge." ([@ 19:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1186s))
- **Move fast.** "when you really know the probability of success is zero, most important thing is to stop wasting time." ([@ 9:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=566s))

**What he's done:** When a cofounder leaves, Seibel says he usually talks to the departing founder first and argues for leaving the equity with the team that stays. He also points to YC's written breakup standards, so both founders get the same advice from him.

**Put into steps (my summary of his advice):**
1. Tell both lawyers to stop sending letters.
2. The two of you agree the terms directly: a no-fault split, he keeps about 1–2%, you pay reasonable severance if you have the money, and neither of you disparages the other or contacts investors.
3. Have one lawyer draft the clean paperwork, and finish within a week.

**What would change his answer:**
- **Misconduct.** If your cofounder broke the law or did something unethical, none of this applies. In that case Seibel says "I would call the lawyers." ([@ 22:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1346s))
- **Real traction.** The advice assumes no product-market fit. If the company were worth something, the percentages would change.
- **Nobody is continuing the company.** His equity numbers assume someone keeps building. If you're both walking away, the stock matters even less and the fight makes even less sense.

One note from me: Seibel's percentages are a rule of thumb for negotiating, not a legal right. If the shares have vested, they belong to your cofounder, and he only gives them back if he agrees to. That's why Seibel's approach starts with persuading the leaver rather than overpowering him.

**Your premise is wrong. Garry Tan didn't say this; Sam Altman did.** It was in Altman's conversation with Tan that closed Startup School 2026 (July 2026). Altman pointed out that Tan couldn't say it himself, since Tan runs YC: "I I can say this, Gary probably can't. I I I think the premium on doing YC is bigger now than it's like ever been before. Uh, the distance between like YC and second place is has expanded." ([yt-ZIaOBAjvc38 @ 16:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s); by: altman)

**Verdict:** Altman's reason is network effects. YC is the best place to meet the people you'll start companies with, and a network like that compounds, so the leader keeps pulling further ahead of second place.

**Based on:** said it (Altman's own words). He offers no numbers for the gap.

**Why he says it**
- **He names network effects as the cause.** Right after the claim he says: "And this is a reminder of the power of network effects." ([@ 16:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s)–[17:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1048s))
- **The context is finding co-founders.** He says that five or ten years earlier, "what felt like was limiting the number of good startups YC could fund is figuring out how to solve the co-founder matching problem". Talented people "just couldn't find their tribe" ([@ 16:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=985s)). In his view, the network is what fixes that.
- **Networks take years to pay off.** He met the people he started OpenAI with "like many many years in some cases before uh starting OpenAI". So "the sooner you can put yourself just in a flow where you're going to meet the people that will be your eventual co-founders … I I think the better. It takes a long time to compound." ([@ 17:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1048s))
- **It's the same reasoning as moving to the Bay Area.** Telling founders to move to San Francisco "used to be very heretical … And looking back, it was clearly right", because there "magic happened. You got a lot of like lucky chances and collisions." ([@ 16:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=985s), [@ 16:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s))

**What Tan actually said:** He made a softer point about the network, without claiming YC is pulling ahead: "someone in this room is going to meet someone else that you're going to start a company with" ([@ 23:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1383s)). He also said "this is the kind of like loose network and the spirit of helping each other and this like very long-term outlook has been an awesome thing." ([@ 23:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1415s); by: tan)

**Paul Graham reaches the same view on his own** (Sept 2026 essay): "YC itself is an instance of network effects in something you wouldn't expect to have them. We didn't intend it to be, but we realized very quickly that that was what we'd stumbled upon." ([web-19ac0b6d18d2](vaults/yc/wiki/startups/strategy/inducing-network-effects.md)). In *Superlinear Returns* (2023) he also wrote that "in a market with network effects, a company that grows fast enough can shut out potential competitors." That second quote is PG's general rule. Altman didn't apply it to YC himself; I'm linking the two.

**What would change his answer:** Altman hedges on the related point about place. He said he has "less of an intuition for it now" and doesn't know if it will hold for the next 10 years ([@ 16:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s)). My own inference, which he didn't say: since his case rests entirely on the network, a rival network that matched founders as well would weaken the claim.

**Caveat:** A former YC president said this on stage at YC's own event, and he gave no data. "I can say this, Gary probably can't" admits the conflict of interest without removing it.

The vault shows she said the opposite. In her 2018 talk, "aggressive" and "ruthless" describe the other investors of that era, and she sets herself and YC against them. The founders she backed were the earnest ones, and she turned down applicants she thought were conceited.

**Based on:** something she said (her 2018 Female Founders Conference talk), with her 2024 Lightcone interview agreeing.

**Where the words come from**
- Her full line: "it felt like a family and I was its mom I was soft and sensitive at a time when investors tended to be hardened and aggressive and I'll throw in ruthless - for a couple of them that I know I cared about how founders were feeling" ([yt-8d-cApFHjeY @ 17:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1064s)). The ruthless people in that sentence are investors.

**What she says she actually looked for**
- She judged character, not ideas: "did they seem earnest did they seem determined were they flexible minded and most importantly what was the relationship between the co-founders like" ([@ 14:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s)).
- She was strict about it: "from the beginning I was very careful about only funding earnest people" (@ 14:51). Also: "if I could tell someone was a conceited we did not fund them … early on I was pretty rigid about this and I think that's the basis of the culture of our alumni community" ([@ 15:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=927s)).
- In 2024 she said the same thing: "Earnest and not pretentious that's in YC's DNA" ([yt-6u4JVz7iQTY @ 45:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=2734s)).

**The toughness she did want**
She wanted grit, not ruthlessness:
- She wanted founders who were "determined" (2018).
- She also wanted them independent-minded: "you cannot be conventional minded to start a startup with a brand new idea" ([yt-6u4JVz7iQTY @ 51:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=3069s)).
- And bold under ridicule: "you do need a certain amount of boldness to work on ideas that most people would consider stupid and to keep going when you're ridiculed or ignored" ([yt-8d-cApFHjeY @ 25:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1545s)).

**Why she thinks her way worked**
- She says she and PG were "not driven by money" (@ 18:52). Having no LPs "allowed us to take more risks with who we chose to fund and it also allowed us to be benevolent to failing startups" (@ 19:26). This put YC at odds with investors who squeezed founders.

**The nearest thing in the vault to the claim** comes from Paul Graham, not Livingston.
- He describes YC's word "formidable" as "someone who gets what they want in any situation" ([yt-5bxp78i96S8 @ 9:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=597s)). He says it comes from his and Jessica's private language.
- Even he links YC's founders to empathy, not ruthlessness: "That kind of empathy is what we look for in founders, and what we cultivate in the ones we accept" ([How to Earn a Billion Dollars](https://paulgraham.com/earn.html), 2026).

**What would change this:** a source where Livingston herself praises ruthless founders. None of the YC vault's sources has one. If you got the claim from a particular article or clip, send it and I can check whether it misquotes the 17:44 line.
